name: Beliefs about God and Texts

objectives.text: Identify that Jewish people believe there is one God who made everything
Name the Torah as the holy scroll read in the synagogue and describe how it is handled with great care
Explain why many Jewish people avoid saying or fully writing God's name and connect this practice to the third commandment
Recognize several Hebrew letters and identify that the Hebrew Scriptures are written mostly in Hebrew and read from right to left
Recite the opening words of the Shema and explain what it teaches about God being one and about loving him with all of life
List the three parts of the Tanakh as Torah, Prophets, and Writings and give an example book from each part
Explain what the Talmud is and distinguish the Mishnah from the Gemara as layers of rabbinic teaching
Describe the Jewish belief that God's covenants with Abraham and with Israel at Sinai form the foundation of Jewish peoplehood
Compare the Jewish understanding of God's oneness with the doctrine of the Trinity as confessed by Reformed churches
Explain the rabbinic teaching that an Oral Torah was given at Sinai alongside the Written Torah
Describe the concept of mitzvot, including the traditional count of 613 commandments, and explain why Judaism views Torah as a whole way of life
Summarize the main points of Maimonides' Thirteen Principles of Faith as a historic statement of Jewish belief about God, Torah, and the Messiah
Explain how the Jewish description of God's character in the thirteen attributes of mercy draws on God's self-revelation to Moses
Explain how religious leadership in Judaism shifted from Temple priests to rabbis as teachers of Torah after the destruction of the Temple in AD 70
Analyze Jesus' disputes with the Pharisees over the tradition of the elders in light of the developing Oral Law
Explain how Midrash and classic commentators such as Rashi interpret passages of the Hebrew Scriptures
Explain the Jewish view of sin and atonement without a Temple through repentance, prayer, good deeds, and Yom Kippur
Compare how Orthodox, Conservative, and Reform Judaism understand the authority of the Written Torah and the Oral Law
Compare the Jewish understanding of righteousness through covenant faithfulness and repentance with the Reformed doctrine of justification by grace through faith in Christ's sacrifice
Evaluate the rabbinic claim of an authoritative oral tradition from Sinai in light of the Reformed doctrine that Scripture alone is the supreme rule of faith
Develop a research study comparing Jewish and Reformed Christian understandings of Israel as God's chosen people using the relevant biblical texts

changes: Kept and reworded the real competencies (one God, Torah scroll, reverence for God's name, Hebrew, Shema, Talmud, Trinity comparison, mitzvot, rabbi and priest, Oral Law and Jesus, atonement without a Temple, salvation comparison, Talmudic tradition, chosen people). Reframed the salvation comparison to describe the Jewish view fairly and reframed the Talmud evaluation around the authority of oral tradition versus sola Scriptura. Dropped 'apply respect for Jewish roots' as an attitude rather than an assessable competency. Dropped the Isaiah 53 objective because Christian readings of the Hebrew Scriptures belong to the sibling sub-topic on Judaism's relationship to the Old Testament. Added the three parts of the Tanakh, covenant as the basis of peoplehood, the Oral Torah concept, Maimonides' Thirteen Principles, the thirteen attributes of mercy, Midrash and Rashi, and the views of the Jewish movements on Torah authority. Replaced Westminster Confession 8.4 with confession articles that state the doctrines taught (WCF 1.2, 1.6, 1.8, 1.10, 2.3, 7.5, 7.6, 11.1, 20.2, WSC Q4, Q5, Q6, Q54, HC Q60) and added verse-level Scripture anchors.
